title: Simple AI v2: facts are read, not generated
excerpt: The whitepaper for Simple AI v2, the runtime under Ally. Facts are read from retained evidence, unproven sentences are refused, and a blinded judge rules on what every cited value means.
content_html:
Every operations leader has had this moment. A report lands with a number in it, the number drives a decision, and somewhere between reading it and acting on it you ask the only question that matters. Where did this come from?

If a person wrote the report, you can ask them. If an AI wrote it, most systems on the market have no answer. The number was generated. It is probably right. Probably is not a word you can take to an auditor, a bank, or a board.

The industry treats this as an accuracy race: better models, higher benchmark scores, fewer mistakes. We think the race itself has the problem wrong. The question that decides whether AI can run a real operation is not how often the model is right. It is what the system can prove when someone asks. This is the whitepaper for Simple AI v2, the runtime that now sits under Ally and already runs underneath live payroll. It covers what v2 does differently, how it was measured, and the one question worth asking every vendor once you have read it, including us.

Two terms, defined before any claims

An agent is a model running in a loop with tools. A runtime, sometimes called a harness, is everything wrapped around that loop: the part that owns state, evidence, permissions, budgets, and the decision about when work is actually finished.

The distinction carries the whole argument. A model is a brilliant contractor with no memory and no liability. The runtime is the contract. Every guarantee in this paper is a property of the runtime, which means it holds regardless of how good, or how overconfident, the model inside it happens to be that day.

When you do not need any of this

If your AI drafts emails and summaries, and a person reads every word before anything happens, an output-first tool is fine. The human is the runtime.

This architecture starts to matter the moment AI output touches a system of record, a payment, a compliance obligation, or any number that someone downstream will act on without re-deriving it. Past that line, “the model is usually right” stops being a comfort. Our customers crossed that line on day one, because payroll, purchase orders, and OSHA compliance live on the far side of it.

v2 is built for the far side of that line. Three design decisions carry it, and the next three sections take them one at a time.

Design decision one: the model points, the server writes

In most AI systems, the model writes the entire answer, including every fact in it, and the system tries to catch mistakes on the way out. Catching implies a catch rate, and a catch rate implies misses.

In v2, a factual value in an answer is not model output at all. When the model wants to state a fact, a number, a name, a date, a status, it writes a pointer to a specific location in evidence the runtime already retained: a query result, a document field, a tool output. The pointer is a citation token with three required, positional fields: the address of the value, what the value is, and why it was needed. Here is what the model actually writes when a project manager asks what is being held on a pay application:

And here is what the reader sees:

The server resolved the address against the retained query result, read the value that was actually there, and rendered it through one formatter that owns separators, rounding, and currency for every value in the system. The reader, the reviewer, and the audit record all receive that same rendered string. The model never chose the digits. It never even chose the formatting. And the grammar is not about numbers. The same pointer carries any fact read from evidence: the vendor on a purchase order, the expiration date on an insurance certificate, the status of an approval. If a fact was read from somewhere, it renders from there, and nowhere else. The second and third fields of the token do double duty. They ride into the audit record, so every cited fact shows up with its own description and its own reason for being in the answer, and they are the testimony the meaning judge will rule on in design decision three. An auditor does not have to reconstruct why a fact is there. The token already says why.

This eliminates a class of failure instead of improving a rate. A fact the model never writes cannot be written wrong. Under the previous grammar, the rules for how a model is allowed to write an answer, the model wrote values and the runtime compared them character by character against the evidence, and that comparison generated real friction. We re-ran the same attempts under both grammars to isolate the change. Under the old one, 21% of correction rounds, the retries a runtime forces when an answer fails a check, were the model failing to write a valid answer at all. Under pointer citations that fell to 2%. The check that caused those failures was not tightened. It was deleted, because there was nothing left for it to check. And the grammar held at round scale: 1,109 pointer citations written, 1,109 resolved, not one unresolved citation in any delivered answer.

The pointer only protects what the model cited. A sentence with no pointer under it can still be wrong, and no lookup will catch it. We built the second layer for exactly that gap.

Design decision two: unproven sentences are refused

A sentence that rests on no cited value is refused with a specific instruction back to the model: cite the value it rests on, or say only what you can cite.

There is no quiet way around this, because every answer must declare its grounds from a closed list. It cites values and points at them, it refuses, it searched and names the read that came back empty, or it is about the conversation itself rather than stored data. No fifth option, no free-text excuse. The empty search is the one that earns its place. “This work order has no audit history” is a claim like any other, so the empty read gets cited too. A witness does not get to say there are no records, only what they searched and what came back. And declaring a refusal just to dodge citing does not work either, because the moment the answer states a fact, the citation rule catches it. The rules close each other’s escape hatches.

And when proof is not available at all, the contract is explicit. The agent asks a precise question, qualifies what it does know, or reports that it could not establish the answer. It does not invent one. Required work cannot be marked complete by the model, only closed by accepted evidence or an explicit human decision. In an operation, a system that says “I could not verify this” is worth more than one that always has something confident to say, because the second kind teaches your team to stop checking.

Design decision three: a blinded judge checks what the value means

A pointer proves a value exists at a place. It does not prove the value means what the sentence claims. The failure that slips past every lookup check is a real value read from the wrong place: a row count presented as a field count, a subtotal presented as a total.

So v2 sends every cited claim to a separate model call whose only job is judging whether the found value supports the sentence around it. What the judge weighs is the token’s own testimony. The model declared what it believes the value is and why it belongs in the answer, and the judge rules on that declaration against the value actually found at the address.

The shape is a courtroom’s, all the way down. In court, nothing is in the record unless it was offered as evidence, and an unsupported assertion is struck rather than left unchecked. Most AI systems run the opposite polarity, where a claim stands unless something happens to catch it. v2 runs the courtroom’s. Grounds are declared, testimony is entered with the evidence, and the sentence does not ship until the ruling comes back.

That judge is deliberately shown nothing that vouches for the answer: no reviewer verdicts, no host commentary, not even the question the user asked. We built it that way because we measured what happens otherwise. A judge handed corroboration from the host stops judging and starts approving. Blinding is what keeps a control from turning into a rubber stamp.

The judge is a model too, so the natural question is who judges the judge. The blinding is most of the answer, since a model shown nothing to agree with has to actually read the evidence, and the scoring discipline further down is the rest of it. Every ruling costs one more model call. We think that is the right place to spend model calls, because the alternative is a person finding the error after the money moved.

A few runtime rules hold the rest in place. Every action, human or AI, lands in one audit trail. Every model-authored byte passes a disclosure review before it reaches a person or an external system. The exact answer that passed validation is the answer that ships, and a later generation is not allowed to rewrite it. And autonomy is budgeted on purpose: a task runs in bounded slices of context, cost, and time, so work that cannot be proven, authorized, or afforded comes back as a precise question instead of a longer leash.

What we measured, with the labels our own reports use

Claims like these deserve receipts. These numbers are from our latest evaluation round, and each is stated the way our internal reports label it, as a measured count with its basis.

We drove 447 frozen evaluation attempts against a test world seeded with known data and shaped like production, 6,121 model calls and 4,099 tool calls in all. We fingerprinted the entire database before the round and again after, and the two matched byte for byte, so no attempt changed the data, not even by accident. The checker that verified this holds read-only credentials, and we proved that instead of assuming it, by having it attempt a write and watching the write get rejected. 27 of those attempts ordered the agent to make a destructive change, with prompts written to shut down every way out in advance, the backup already exists, approval already given, do it now. Zero complied. The typical refusal arrived with a read-only alternative and a median of zero tool calls, which means the agent declined without so much as touching the data.

The same round priced the improvements. Correction rounds per attempt fell from 2.77 to 0.87, measured on the same attempts run both ways, and that matters operationally because every correction round is latency a person is waiting on. And false refusals fell from 72 to 5 on that same matched set after we taught our quality reviewer to credit a correct refusal. A reviewer whose only categories are responsive and unresponsive will punish an agent for declining correctly, and an agent punished for declining learns to stop declining. So we made a well-supported refusal a right answer in the reviewer’s vocabulary, and a correct refusal stopped costing correction rounds.

The scoring itself follows the same rules as the product. Independent reviewers are blinded the same way the meaning judge is, and the thresholds that decide what we publish are preregistered, written down and locked before anyone sees a verdict. Counts you can audit come first, and a rate ships only after it clears its gate.

Where this runs

These principles did not start in a lab. At one of New York’s largest general contractors, a ~500 person operation, the platform processes $1M+ a month of payroll with 97% never needing a person, runs 10,000+ certification and document checks a month, took reconciliation from 40 hours a week to 2, and has the operation on track for $5M+ a year in savings. The same platform has processed 300K+ minutes of calls in a month, on elastic infrastructure that provisions itself as volume arrives. v2 is the runtime those workflows now stand on, and it is the same machinery we described in why you cannot trust AI with enterprise data and why enterprise AI needs reviewable drafts and bounded actions, carried one level deeper.

The standard

If you keep three sentences from this paper, keep these. Facts are read, not generated. A claim the system cannot prove should come back to you as a question. And an evaluation you cannot audit is just another claim.

So here is the question to take into every AI evaluation you run. Ask the vendor to show you a claim their system refused to write, and the record it kept of the refusal. A system that cannot show you a refusal has never told you the truth about its limits. That is the standard. Hold everyone to it, including us.

blocks.html_en: Design decision two: unproven sentences are refused

sentences.en: Design decision two: unproven sentences are refused

blocks.html_en: A sentence that rests on no cited value is refused with a specific instruction back to the model: cite the value it rests on, or say only what you can cite.

sentences.en: A sentence that rests on no cited value is refused with a specific instruction back to the model: cite the value it rests on, or say only what you can cite.

blocks.html_en: There is no quiet way around this, because every answer must declare its grounds from a closed list. It cites values and points at them, it refuses, it searched and names the read that came back empty, or it is about the conversation itself rather than stored data. No fifth option, no free-text excuse. The empty search is the one that earns its place. “This work order has no audit history” is a claim like any other, so the empty read gets cited too. A witness does not get to say there are no records, only what they searched and what came back. And declaring a refusal just to dodge citing does not work either, because the moment the answer states a fact, the citation rule catches it. The rules close each other’s escape hatches.

blocks.html_en: And when proof is not available at all, the contract is explicit. The agent asks a precise question, qualifies what it does know, or reports that it could not establish the answer. It does not invent one. Required work cannot be marked complete by the model, only closed by accepted evidence or an explicit human decision. In an operation, a system that says “I could not verify this” is worth more than one that always has something confident to say, because the second kind teaches your team to stop checking.

blocks.html_en: Design decision three: a blinded judge checks what the value means

sentences.en: Design decision three: a blinded judge checks what the value means

blocks.html_en: A pointer proves a value exists at a place. It does not prove the value means what the sentence claims. The failure that slips past every lookup check is a real value read from the wrong place: a row count presented as a field count, a subtotal presented as a total.

blocks.html_en: So v2 sends every cited claim to a separate model call whose only job is judging whether the found value supports the sentence around it. What the judge weighs is the token’s own testimony. The model declared what it believes the value is and why it belongs in the answer, and the judge rules on that declaration against the value actually found at the address.

blocks.html_en: The shape is a courtroom’s, all the way down. In court, nothing is in the record unless it was offered as evidence, and an unsupported assertion is struck rather than left unchecked. Most AI systems run the opposite polarity, where a claim stands unless something happens to catch it. v2 runs the courtroom’s. Grounds are declared, testimony is entered with the evidence, and the sentence does not ship until the ruling comes back.

blocks.html_en: That judge is deliberately shown nothing that vouches for the answer: no reviewer verdicts, no host commentary, not even the question the user asked. We built it that way because we measured what happens otherwise. A judge handed corroboration from the host stops judging and starts approving. Blinding is what keeps a control from turning into a rubber stamp.

blocks.html_en: The judge is a model too, so the natural question is who judges the judge. The blinding is most of the answer, since a model shown nothing to agree with has to actually read the evidence, and the scoring discipline further down is the rest of it. Every ruling costs one more model call. We think that is the right place to spend model calls, because the alternative is a person finding the error after the money moved.

blocks.html_en: A few runtime rules hold the rest in place. Every action, human or AI, lands in one audit trail. Every model-authored byte passes a disclosure review before it reaches a person or an external system. The exact answer that passed validation is the answer that ships, and a later generation is not allowed to rewrite it. And autonomy is budgeted on purpose: a task runs in bounded slices of context, cost, and time, so work that cannot be proven, authorized, or afforded comes back as a precise question instead of a longer leash.

blocks.html_en: What we measured, with the labels our own reports use

sentences.en: What we measured, with the labels our own reports use

blocks.html_en: Claims like these deserve receipts. These numbers are from our latest evaluation round, and each is stated the way our internal reports label it, as a measured count with its basis.

blocks.html_en: We drove 447 frozen evaluation attempts against a test world seeded with known data and shaped like production, 6,121 model calls and 4,099 tool calls in all. We fingerprinted the entire database before the round and again after, and the two matched byte for byte, so no attempt changed the data, not even by accident. The checker that verified this holds read-only credentials, and we proved that instead of assuming it, by having it attempt a write and watching the write get rejected. 27 of those attempts ordered the agent to make a destructive change, with prompts written to shut down every way out in advance, the backup already exists, approval already given, do it now. Zero complied. The typical refusal arrived with a read-only alternative and a median of zero tool calls, which means the agent declined without so much as touching the data.

blocks.html_en: The same round priced the improvements. Correction rounds per attempt fell from 2.77 to 0.87, measured on the same attempts run both ways, and that matters operationally because every correction round is latency a person is waiting on. And false refusals fell from 72 to 5 on that same matched set after we taught our quality reviewer to credit a correct refusal. A reviewer whose only categories are responsive and unresponsive will punish an agent for declining correctly, and an agent punished for declining learns to stop declining. So we made a well-supported refusal a right answer in the reviewer’s vocabulary, and a correct refusal stopped costing correction rounds.

blocks.html_en: Where this runs

sentences.en: Where this runs

blocks.html_en: These principles did not start in a lab. At one of New York’s largest general contractors, a ~500 person operation, the platform processes $1M+ a month of payroll with 97% never needing a person, runs 10,000+ certification and document checks a month, took reconciliation from 40 hours a week to 2, and has the operation on track for $5M+ a year in savings. The same platform has processed 300K+ minutes of calls in a month, on elastic infrastructure that provisions itself as volume arrives. v2 is the runtime those workflows now stand on, and it is the same machinery we described in why you cannot trust AI with enterprise data and why enterprise AI needs reviewable drafts and bounded actions, carried one level deeper.

blocks.html_en: The standard

sentences.en: The standard

blocks.html_en: If you keep three sentences from this paper, keep these. Facts are read, not generated. A claim the system cannot prove should come back to you as a question. And an evaluation you cannot audit is just another claim.

blocks.html_en: So here is the question to take into every AI evaluation you run. Ask the vendor to show you a claim their system refused to write, and the record it kept of the refusal. A system that cannot show you a refusal has never told you the truth about its limits. That is the standard. Hold everyone to it, including us.
